title: arrival-smoothing-and-batch-formation-profiles
content:
Purpose:
This note collects a set of lightweight experiments exploring arrival-rate smoothing (EWMA) and batch-formation heuristics for the continuous batching scheduler. Goal is to find settings that keep P95/P99 tail latency acceptable while preserving batch fill-rates (cost) and soft fairness across client classes. This is a working doc — lots of rough numbers and TODOs.

Context / baseline:
- Runtime: serving-runtime v2.4.1 (linux,A100-80GB nodes, CUDA 12.2 kernels)
- Baseline scheduler: immediate-first-come, max_batch=32, timeout_ms=20, no explicit age bias; measured with synthetic replay harness (1M requests per run).
- Workload mixes: bursty arrival (Poisson with bursts), steady low-QPS, mixed priority classes (class A high-qps, class B low-qps). Sequence length buckets: short(32 tok)=60%, med(128)=30%, long(512)=10%.
- Measurement: 5 runs per config, warmup 100k requests, reported numbers are medians across runs.

Key knobs explored:
- arrival_smoothing_alpha (EWMA on observed arrival rate): 0.05, 0.2, 0.5
- max_batch_size: 8, 16, 32, 64
- timeout_ms (batch formation timeout): 5, 10, 20, 50
- age_bias (per-request increment added to priority score to address starvation): 0.0, 0.4, 1.0
- fairness_mode: none | class-aware | age-weighted

Experiment matrix (representative subset):
1) EWMA alpha=0.05, max_batch=64, timeout=50ms, age_bias=0.0, fairness=none
   - avg batch fill-rate: 0.82
   - P50/P95/P99 latency (ms): 9 / 34 / 210
   - comments: large batches and long timeout maximize throughput but P99 explodes on bursts (210ms) due to queueing of long requests, high variance.

2) EWMA alpha=0.5 (fast-react), max_batch=32, timeout=20ms, age_bias=0.0
   - fill-rate: 0.65
   - P50/P95/P99: 7 / 28 / 90
   - comments: faster reaction reduces large tails; lower fill-rate increases cost per token.

3) EWMA alpha=0.2, max_batch=16, timeout=10ms, age_bias=0.4 (age-weighted fairness)
   - fill-rate: 0.58
   - P50/P95/P99: 6 / 22 / 45
   - fairness: class-B 99th latency reduced by ~40% vs (2); class-A median increased ~10%
   - comments: age-bias helps tail for low-volume clients without catastrophic impact on high-volume clients. This is a promising middle-ground.

4) alpha=0.2, max_batch=8, timeout=5ms, age_bias=1.0 (strong age bias)
   - fill-rate: 0.41
   - P50/P95/P99: 5 / 18 / 34
   - cost impact: per-token overhead +24% vs baseline (max_batch=32)
   - comments: strong bias keeps tails low but throughput cost rises sharply — likely expensive in production.

Profiling notes (where time goes):
- enqueue path (scheduler) median: 0.12ms per request (lock contention visible when QPS per core > 12k)
- batch assembly and metadata copy: 0.43ms median, spikes to >2ms when copying KV cache pointers for long sequences
- serialization + RPC send: 0.9ms median (dominant for short sequences when GPU inference is fast)
- kernel launch overhead (per-batch): ~0.8ms for small batches on some CUDA drivers; batched kernels reduce this but not fully eliminated
- per-request age scoring: negligible (<0.05ms) until used in complex priority queues where heap ops show up (~0.3ms under contention)
- note: our profiler shows a recurring 1.6ms GC-like pause in the scheduler thread on some nodes — uninvestigated.

Tradeoffs observed (summary):
- Bigger batches -> better tokens/sec and cost but increases P99 dramatically under bursty arrivals due to queueing delay; this effect is amplified when long sequences are present (long seqs occupy GPU slots).
- Larger timeout slightly improves fill-rate but tail latency increases almost linearly once timeout >20ms for our burst profile.
- Faster arrival smoothing (higher alpha) helps reduce tail by reacting quicker to drops in arrival rate; downside is more variability in batch sizes (fill-rate drop).
- Age-based biasing reduces starvation for sparse clients and brings down their P99 by a lot with modest impact on global P50; strong biasing increases unit cost (smaller batches).
- Fairness modes that partition capacity (strict class-aware allocation) guarantee tail SLA but can underutilize GPU when partitions are idle. Age-weighted dynamic fairness hit best practical tradeoffs.

Representative numbers (normalized cost and tail):
- Baseline (max_batch=32, timeout=20, no-age): cost_index=1.00, global P99=90ms
- Age-weighted (parameters from 3): cost_index=1.12, global P99=45ms, class-B P99 down 40%
- Aggressive batching (case 1): cost_index=0.78, global P99=210ms (bad for SLAs)

Operational considerations:
- Canary rollout plan: implement age-weighted mode behind runtime flag, roll to 5% traffic for 24h, monitor P50/P95/P99 per-customer and token cost. If class-B P99 improves without >10% cost regression, expand.
- Instrumentation additions needed: per-request enqueue timestamp (already present), per-batch assembly duration histogram, per-class age distribution, lock contention counters, and scheduler-thread STW pause detection.
- Synthetic harness improvements: add interleaved long-sequence spikes, multi-tenant churn (lots of tiny clients starting/stopping) and cache-warmup scenarios to better exercise starvation cases.

Open hypotheses / questions:
- Is the 1.6ms pause scheduler-side due to periodic stats flush or Java agent? (trace local node to confirm).
- Can we reduce copying cost by passing KV cache references into batch assembly instead of duplicating structures? Microbenchmark suggests ~0.6ms saved for long sequences if feasible.
- Would a deferred-launch strategy (launch cheap lightweight pre-kernel to reserve GPU lane) reduce kernel-launch overhead for small batches? Potential driver/kernel complexity.

Immediate next steps (actionable):
- Samir: add per-batch assembly histograms and lock-wait counters to the scheduler (PR link: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1012) — due 2026-03-05
- Jia: run extended synthetic replay with churn + long spikes for top 4 promising configs (3x 2M requests) and upload artifact to the confluence page linked above — due 2026-03-09
- Tom: investigate scheduler 1.6ms pause on a repro node, collect traces and rule out stats flush — due 2026-03-07
- Owner (me): prepare canary toggles and rollout runbook if Jia's extended runs show consistent improvements.

Notes-to-self / loose ideas:
- Consider hybrid: allow max_batch=64 but enforce a dynamic per-tenant cap during burst windows to avoid one tenant causing system-wide P99 spikes.
- Try asymmetric timeout: shorter timeout when current batch contains at least one long-sequence request (reduces head-of-line blocking).
- Evaluate cost-vs-quality metric that weights P99 more heavily for paid customers when autoscaling cost is considered.

Appendix: example raw run output (one run):
- Config: alpha=0.2, max_batch=16, timeout=10, age_bias=0.4
- Requests: 1,000,000 (60/30/10 seq dist), warmup 100k
- Batch size distribution: 1:12%, 2-4:35%, 5-8:28%, 9-16:25%
- Fill-rate: 0.58
- Latency (ms): mean 14.6, median 6.0, P95 22.3, P99 44.8
- Scheduler CPU usage: 48% on single core (pinned), scheduler thread sysread spikes align with long-sequence spikes.

If you read this and want different slices of the matrix, add a line to the TODOs. This doc should live with other serving-runtime quick experiments; move to final notes when we lock config for canary.

-- Elena
